# Global Compensation Policy Design: A "Localize the Base, Globalize the Rest" Framework

## 1. Diagnosing the Actual Problem

The friction isn't really about pay bands — it's about three colliding forces:

- **Perception:** Employees compare *nominal* salaries across borders, not competitive position within markets. Warsaw engineers see a Berlin number, not a percentile.
- **Data volatility:** Remote work has made some talent markets (senior engineering, ML/AI) genuinely global, while others remain local. Static survey data can't keep up.
- **Regulation:** The EU Pay Transparency Directive (transposition deadline June 2026), US state posting laws, and similar regimes mean your internal gaps will be visible whether you publish them or not. **Secrecy is no longer an available strategy — only defensibility is.**

The design goal: a system where every pay difference can be explained by an objective, documented, legally defensible criterion.

---

## 2. Five Design Principles

1. **One company, one job architecture.** Leveling, expectations, and career paths are identical everywhere. This is both a fairness anchor and a legal requirement (the EU directive's "work of equal value" test).
2. **Pay follows the market you actually compete in** — not cost of living, not nationality. This single rule resolves most edge cases.
3. **Compress, don't equalize.** Full location-agnostic pay across 30 countries is cost-prohibitive and creates local market distortion; pure market-rate pay creates unbearable internal gaps. Deliberately narrow the spread.
4. **Globalize everything except base salary.** Equity, bonus targets, and benefits floors are the "one company" signal.
5. **Publish by default.** Transparency is cheaper than the appearance of concealment under disclosure laws.

---

## 3. The Policy Architecture

### 3.1 Global Job Architecture (the compliance backbone)
- Single leveling framework (e.g., IC1–IC7, M3–M6) with gender-neutral evaluation criteria: skills, effort, responsibility, working conditions — exactly what the EU directive requires for "equal value" comparisons.
- Every pay decision must trace to level + market data + performance. No undocumented exceptions.

### 3.2 Segment Roles by Talent-Market Scope
This is the key innovation that resolves the Warsaw/Lisbon vs. Berlin/Toronto tension:

| Role category | Examples | Pay treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **Global-market roles** | Senior+ engineers, ML/AI, security — roles where you compete with US-remote employers | **Single global band** (~90–100% of US market rate) regardless of location |
| **Regional-market roles** | Support, ops, finance, most G&A | Zone-based bands (below) |

When a Warsaw engineer asks why a peer earns more, the answer is a *rule*, not a judgment: "If we compete for your role globally, we pay you globally." It also creates a self-correcting mechanism — if attrition data shows a role's market has gone global, it moves to the global band at the next review.

### 3.3 Zone Model with Compressed Differentials (regional roles)
Replace 30 country-specific bands with **3–4 zones**, which depersonalizes comparisons ("your market cluster," not "your country"):

| Zone | Illustrative markets | Index vs. Zone 1 | Pure market would be |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SF/NY, Zurich, London | 100% | 100% |
| 2 | Berlin, Toronto, Amsterdam | ~85–90% | ~80–85% |
| 3 | Warsaw, Lisbon, Prague, Madrid | ~72–80% | ~55–65% |
| 4 | Emerging markets | ~55–65% | ~45–55% |

The compression mechanism: target the **50th–60th percentile in expensive markets** and the **65th–75th percentile in lower-cost markets**. You deliberately overpay relative to local market in Zone 3/4 — buying retention and fairness goodwill at a fraction of the cost of full equalization. Add a **global floor** (no professional band minimum below a set threshold, e.g., ~€38k equivalent).

### 3.4 Band-Setting Methodology (taming the data problem)
- **Triangulate three sources:** one traditional survey (Mercer/WTW/Radford), one real-time platform (Pave, Carta, Levels.fyi), plus your own offer/attrition data. Weight ~50/30/20.
- **Smoothing rule:** apply only 50% of indicated market movement per cycle, capped at ±10%. Bands never decrease in nominal local currency — hot markets cool via slower growth, not cuts.
- **FX collar:** bands maintained in local currency; adjust only on cumulative currency moves >8%, reviewed semi-annually. No monthly whiplash.
- **Full documentation trail** for every band decision — this becomes your legal evidence of "objective, gender-neutral criteria."

### 3.5 Total Rewards Mix
- **Equity: identical grant value (USD) by level, globally.** Equal equity is the strongest fairness signal available and costs nothing extra in high-cost markets.
- **Bonus: same target % of base by level, globally.**
- **Benefits: global floor** (minimum leave, parental leave, health standard) + local top-ups for statutory requirements.

### 3.6 Mobility Rules (the remote-work flashpoint)
- Voluntary relocation to a lower zone: **base held flat, never cut**; future increases moderated until the band catches up. Equity untouched.
- Company-initiated moves: never downward.
- Temporary stays (<90 days): no adjustment.

---

## 4. Transparency & Legal Compliance Layer

Design to the **strictest applicable standard globally** — it's simpler than 30 patchwork policies:

- **Salary ranges in every job posting, everywhere** (satisfies EU PTD and US state laws simultaneously).
- **No salary-history questions; no pay-secrecy clauses** in any contract (both banned under the EU directive anyway).
- **EU PTD readiness:** worker right-to-information requests apply at *any* company size — build an HRIS workflow with a response SLA; prepare for pay-gap reporting thresholds (250+ employees from 2027) and the **joint pay assessment** trigger (unjustified gap ≥5% in any category).
- **Annual third-party pay equity audit** controlling for level, function, tenure, performance, location. Remediate unexplained gaps above ~2% immediately, with a reserved budget (~0.5–1% of payroll). Audit *before* you're forced to disclose.
- **Works council consultation** (Germany, France, etc.) started early — it's a rollout gate, not an afterthought.
- Note: cross-border comparisons are generally *not* valid legal comparators under EU "single source" doctrine — but don't rely on that. The reputational and retention risk from forum comparisons exists regardless of legal liability.

---

## 5. Managing the Perception Problem Directly

- **Publish the methodology externally** (GitLab/Buffer-style handbook): zones, percentile targets, data sources, the global-band rule. Engineers respect systems they can inspect.
- **Publish internal band tables** so every employee sees their range and compa-ratio, with manager toolkits for pay conversations.
- **Show purchasing-power context neutrally** (OECD PPP data) alongside nominal bands — a Warsaw engineer at the 70th local percentile often has stronger local purchasing power than a Berlin peer at the 55th. Present data; don't argue.
- **Engage forums, never police them.** Quarterly compensation AMAs with the CPO. Attempting to suppress salary discussion is now both illegal in the EU and culturally fatal.
- **Reframe the growth path:** the way to earn more is leveling up (identical criteria everywhere), not relocating.

---

## 6. Rollout Roadmap

| Phase | Timing | Actions |
|---|---|---|
| **0: Stabilize** | 0–90 days | Freeze band exceptions; pay equity audit; listening sessions in Warsaw/Lisbon hotspots; publish existing bands internally; map all 30 countries' disclosure obligations |
| **1: Rebuild** | Q2–Q3 2026 | Job architecture v2; zone model + role segmentation; data methodology; mobility policy; manager training; PTD information-request workflow; begin works council consultation |
| **2: Launch** | Q4 2026 | New bands effective with **grandfathering** (no one cut; above-band employees get lump sums until bands catch up; below-band get accelerated adjustments); external publication of ranges + philosophy; first equalized equity grants |
| **3: Steady state** | 2027 | Dry-run pay gap report; joint-assessment readiness; annual refresh cycle locked to reporting deadlines |

---

## 7. Success Metrics

- Unexplained pay gap <2% (gender and cross-zone, level-controlled)
- 80%+ of employees within compa-ratio 0.9–1.1
- Offer acceptance ≥85% in every zone
- Regretted attrition in Zone 3 hotspots trending down quarter-over-quarter
- ≥70% pulse-survey agreement with "I understand how my pay is determined"
- Zero compliance misses (posting ranges, information-request SLAs)

---

## 8. Honest Trade-offs

- **Cost:** Compression plus global bands for hot roles adds roughly 4–7% to payroll (model before committing). Offset partially by shifting hiring mix toward Zones 3–4, where you're now a top-of-market employer.
- **Two-tier optics:** A global-band engineer sitting (virtually) next to a zone-band marketer requires relentless communication of the market-scope principle.
- **Zone boundary cases:** Portugal vs. Spain-type edge cases will arise — rule: countries change zones only on two consecutive years of data, with transition protection.
- **Transparency will expose legacy sins:** Remediate before publishing wherever possible; it's far cheaper than remediating under a joint pay assessment.

**The bottom line:** you cannot make the numbers equal, and after June 2026 you cannot make them secret. The only viable strategy is to make every difference *explained, documented, and principled* — and to let the global-band rule turn your loudest fairness critics into evidence that the system works.

run.userPrompt:
In 2026, a fully remote software company employs people in 30 countries. Its location-adjusted pay bands, introduced earlier, now generate friction: engineers in Warsaw and Lisbon compare salaries with peers in Berlin and Toronto on public forums, new labor-market data complicates band setting, and several countries now require pay-transparency disclosures that expose internal gaps.

Design a compensation-policy approach for a globally distributed workforce that balances cost-of-labor logic, internal fairness perceptions, and new pay-transparency laws across jurisdictions.
